opus-5.5.text:
I think the holy grail, at least from my perspective, is something like this: you'd like to be able to take a sensitive dataset, run some algorithm on it once, and produce a synthetic dataset that satisfies differential privacy. That synthetic data would then be useful for essentially any downstream analysis or learning task that someone might want to perform, including tasks you didn't anticipate when you generated it.

The reason that's so appealing is that differential privacy has this nice post-processing property. Once you've released something that's differentially private, anything anyone does with it afterward is also private. So if you could release one synthetic dataset, you could hand it to analysts, researchers, and data scientists and say, "Go do whatever you want." You wouldn't need to manage a privacy budget query by query, and you wouldn't need every user to understand differential privacy. They'd just work with what looks like an ordinary dataset.

The catch is that there are real theoretical limits. We've known for a while that you can't preserve the answers to all possible questions with high accuracy while also guaranteeing privacy. There are lower bounds that say if you try to be accurate on too rich a class of queries, you necessarily leak too much. There are also computational hardness results showing that even in cases where it's statistically possible, doing it efficiently can be intractable in the worst case.

So the scientific question becomes more nuanced. For what rich but realistic classes of tasks, such as marginals, linear queries, or the kinds of statistics that a typical machine learning pipeline depends on, can we efficiently generate synthetic data that is simultaneously private and accurate? And can we do that at the scale and dimensionality of real-world data, not just toy problems?

A lot of the exciting recent work, some of which we've been involved in, takes a more practical, almost heuristic stance. You treat synthetic data generation as an optimization problem. You use modern tools like gradient-based methods or learned generative models, and you try to match a large set of statistics subject to a privacy constraint. Empirically, these approaches do surprisingly well, much better than worst-case theory might lead you to fear.

So I'd describe the holy grail as closing the gap between those two worlds. We want principled methods with provable privacy, which we can get, together with meaningful accuracy guarantees across broad, practically relevant families of downstream uses. And they should be computationally feasible on real high-dimensional data. If we could get all three of those at once, I think synthetic data would become a truly transformative tool for sharing sensitive data, in places like the census, healthcare, and finance.

r001.rationale: The response proposes releasing one differentially private synthetic dataset for analysts to use for downstream tasks, avoiding query-by-query privacy-budget management.

r002.rationale: It describes broad downstream usefulness as an aspiration, but narrows the achievable goal to realistic task families and explicitly notes limits on preserving answers to all possible questions. It does not clearly claim guaranteed results similar to the original for arbitrary machine-learning experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the holy grail, if you want to call it that, is pretty easy to state and very hard to achieve. You'd like to be able to take a sensitive dataset, say medical records or financial transactions, and produce a synthetic dataset that is differentially private, so you have a rigorous guarantee that no individual's data can be reverse-engineered from it, and at the same time have that synthetic data be, for all practical purposes, a drop-in replacement for the real data. Meaning any analysis you would have run on the real thing, any statistic you would have computed, any machine learning model you would have trained, you can run on the synthetic data instead and get essentially the same answer.

Now, the reason that's a holy grail and not just an engineering problem is that we know from the theory that you can't have everything. There are lower bounds that say if you want to preserve all possible statistics of a high-dimensional dataset under differential privacy, you'll need an astronomical amount of data, or your accuracy will fall apart. So the realistic version of the goal is more nuanced. You pick a rich but not infinite class of queries you care about, maybe all the low-order marginals, all the correlations between small sets of attributes, and you ask for synthetic data that's simultaneously accurate on all of those. That turns out to be achievable in principle, and there's been real progress on the algorithms, including approaches that borrow from game theory, where you can think of a generator trying to fool an adversary who's hunting for the query where the synthetic data is most wrong.

What's still open, and what I'd personally most like to see, is closing the gap between what the theory says is possible and what runs well in practice on messy, high-dimensional, real-world data. Right now there's often a trade-off where the methods with the best guarantees are computationally painful, and the methods that scale lose some of the rigor. If we could get to the point where a hospital or a census bureau could routinely release a private synthetic version of their data and researchers would actually trust it for discovery, not just for sanity checks, that would be the payoff. And I'd add that the synthetic data framing has a very appealing property compared to interactive query mechanisms: once you've released it, you're done. There's no privacy budget to keep track of, no need to decide in advance who gets to ask what. That's a big part of why I think it's worth chasing.

r001.rationale: It describes releasing the private synthetic dataset once so users can run analyses on it themselves, and contrasts this with interactive query mechanisms that require managing a privacy budget.

r002.rationale: It calls the holy grail a differentially private synthetic dataset that acts as a drop-in replacement, giving essentially the same results for analyses and machine-learning models run on the original data.

astra-6.text:
I think the holy grail is to take a sensitive data set and produce a synthetic version that is differentially private, but that you can then use more or less as you would the original data. You could give it to people who don’t have permission to see the underlying records, and they could explore it, compute statistics, build models, and get approximately the same answers they would have gotten from the real data.

The hard part is making that promise precise. What does it mean to preserve the useful properties of a data set? If you tell me in advance that you care about a particular collection of statistics, that gives me a target. But if you want a synthetic data set that supports any analysis somebody might dream up later, that’s a much stronger requirement, and in general you can’t have that with strong privacy.

So the scientific challenge is understanding how broad a class of analyses we can support, with what accuracy, at what privacy level, and with computationally practical methods. The aspiration is something that feels like a general-purpose substitute for the original data, while being very clear about where that substitution is reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says users can analyze a released synthetic dataset, but does not describe it as replacing an interactive sequence of noisy query answers.

r002.rationale: It describes broad reuse as an aspiration but says supporting any analysis is a stronger requirement that generally cannot be met with strong privacy; it does not identify guaranteed similar results for arbitrary downstream machine-learning experiments as the holy grail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scientific holy grail is to understand when you can generate a synthetic data set that is differentially private and still useful for a broad range of analyses—including analyses you didn’t specify in advance. You’d like to hand somebody a data set that looks like the original in the statistical respects they care about, let them work with it using their usual tools, and have a rigorous privacy guarantee for the individuals in the original data.

The challenge is that you can’t preserve everything. If you ask for accuracy on a sufficiently rich collection of questions, you eventually run into fundamental limitations. So the scientific question is: what structure in the data, or what restrictions on the analyses, make that possible? And can we turn those conditions into computationally practical methods? That combination of broad utility, rigorous privacy, and computational efficiency is really the goal.

r001.rationale: The response says users can analyze a released private dataset themselves, but does not describe it as replacing an interactive sequence of noisy query answers.

r002.rationale: It mentions broad analyses not specified in advance, but does not claim similar results are guaranteed for arbitrary downstream machine-learning experiments; it instead notes limitations and possible restrictions.
